subtopic: PARTICIPATION BY FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENTS

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PARTICIPATION BY FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I propose to avail myself of the opportunity afforded on the discussion of this motion to bring before the house today the discussion of power development and a policy of joint investment by the federal and provincial governments in power development throughout Canada. In raising this subject I am not limiting the purport of the motion to hydroelectric power or to electricity but include the development of industrial power generally, with particular reference to the development of hydroelectric power, underground gasification of coal for power generation purposes and atomic power.
It seems to me that there is no occasion to devote too much time to emphasizing the immense advantages of the development of our available hydroelectric resources. Every Canadian has seen the remarkable results that follow the harnessing of our great streams in this country. There is reason to believe that it may be possible to harness other power besides that of the flowing rivers. Research is now being carried out into the harnessing of tides and the flow of water between confined rocky shores. New possibilities are presented in that field. Particularly, hdwever, all Canadians have had occasion to be tremendously impressed by the consequences that have followed in every case where great water powers have been harnessed.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that in some of the discussions which have taken place publicly in recent months too much emphasis has been placed upon the cost of transmission of electric energy from power sites to the point where the power will be used. I mention that matter for this reason. For example, in relation to the development of certain of our power resources, I have noted that some emphasis has been placed upon the fact that in harnessing those power resources it would cost us a great deal to carry that power to the industrial centres. For instance, I have seen that suggestion made in the case of the greatest power resource we have in Canada, namely
Power Development
Grand falls on the Hamilton river where more than 3 million horsepower are immediately available with the harnessing of those mighty waters. I would suggest that those who think only in terms of carrying power to existing centres of production should examine what has happened out in northern British Columbia. One of the most exciting and challenging developments has taken place at Kitimat, where great water powers have been harnessed in the sub-Arctic, and now one of the largest aluminum plants in the world is producing aluminum as a result of the fact that water power is available at that point. No attempt was made to carry that power long distances by transmission lines. They carried it that relatively short distance, over a mountain it is true but over a comparatively short distance, to the producing site on the seaboard where the processed aluminum could be shipped to the markets of the world. I feel confident that with the harnessing of Grand falls on the Hamilton river, not very far from the great air base of Goose Bay which so many of us know, we will see pulp and paper mills, metal processing and other developments of that kind take place within close proximity to that distant spot.
Nevertheless, even if transmission lines are necessary, the constant improvement of the alloyed metals which carry the power is facilitating more and more every day the transmission of heavy loads of electrical energy to distant points. I mention this because it is not only in the case of the production of electrical energy, but also energy of other kinds, that it would be well if we could keep in our minds the fact that industry goes to power. The largest producer of aluminium at this time is at Shipshaw. In that case bauxite from Jamaica and South America is carried by ship up the St. Lawrence and up the Saguenay to the mill near the tremendous power plant at Shipshaw. The process of production went to the source of power. The same thing happened at Kitimat, as I have mentioned.
In this regard I should like to mention the possible use of some of our vast coal resources in Cape Breton, where no doubt there could be, with the underground gasification of coal, power generation carried out at economic costs. In discussing that, I have seen it stated that there would be very long transmission lines between the place where the power would be produced and Halifax. I should like to emphasize the fact that if power were produced in Cape Breton by the underground gasification of coal in those seams which in some cases are not being worked, it would be possible to instal

Power Development
secondary industries at that point because this power would be produced near the seaboard.
Not only new steel mills but other types of secondary production could be established there from which would be shipped the finished product to the markets of the world. This tremendous possibility of power development presents itself right across Canada. In British Columbia there are enormous power resources waiting to be harnessed. I think that in British Columbia there are perhaps some of the greatest sources of power still waiting to be brought under control and developed for the production of electricity. Our members from British Columbia will be discussing that subject. Our members from the maritime provinces will be discussing this subject from the point of view of development in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and the other maritime provinces.
In addition also to the production of electricity by means of hydro, and the thermal production of electricity, there is the production of electricity by gasification and by atomic energy. Atomic energy is no longer a dream in the production of electricity. This year electricity will be flowing into the great electricity grid in Britain from an atomic plant, and that is only the beginning of a tremendous program, which, in a few years, will be contributing a large quantity of the needed electricity in Britain to their grid system.
In this country experiments are taking place in co-operation between the agencies of the federal government and the Ontario Hydro-Electric Power Commission for ' the purpose of designing and planning atomic energy electricity plants. This presents immense possibilities for the future and particularly for those provinces which nature has not endowed with great natural water resources. This will be of particular importance to the maritime provinces. In the maritime provinces there are water powers but not the mighty rivers that we have in Quebec, in Ontario, in British Columbia and also in some measure in the northern parts of the prairie provinces as well. In the southern part of the prairie provinces and in the maritime provinces there will undoubtedly be a particular interest in the development of atomic energy.
I feel sure that all hon. members have been interested in the report of the citizens' committee in the United States, which was presented to the government of the United States just a few weeks ago. In that report they pictured the possibility that within 25 years more than half of all the electricity used in the United States may come from
fMr. Drew.]
atomic energy. That is how close we actually are to the possibility of the commercial use of atomic energy for the production of electricity. I recognize, and I am not minimizing the fact, that much still needs to be done to bring the production of electricity from atomic energy down to an economic level of production costs. However, it was pointed out by this extremely competent committee, representative of management, of engineering skill, of organized labour and of other activities associated with ventures of this kind, that there is every reason to believe that we are on the brink, if one might use that word without inviting criticism, of great new opportunities in the use of this energy; that we are in fact in all probability just at the beginning of the atomic age so far as the peaceful use of atomic energy is concerned for industrial and power purposes.
In making the recommendations that I propose to make I am not suggesting that the federal government should get into the active production of power in those areas. I am very conscious of the fact, and have reason to be particularly conscious of the fact, that the development of resources is within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provincial governments. Under no circumstances should it be implied or suggested that the federal government will in any way seek to invade that field of responsibility which is that of the provincial governments.
It is already apparent that many of the provincial governments find it necessary to seek financial support in carrying out some of the ventures which they would like to develop within their own boundaries. Some provinces have such a broad financial basis that they are fully capable of undertaking any activities of this kind except in the case of atomic energy. In the case of atomic energy, however, it would seem likely that it will require the co-operation of the federal government in almost every case because of the special relationship of the federal government to the many aspects of atomic energy research.
I do not want anything I say today to be taken as implying that I am suggesting that this government get any further into business.
I think the time has come for this government to divest itself of many of the activities it has taken on, and which it took on for some particular reason. I think that, except for those cases that are manifestly special activities which should be brought under government development, this government would be well advised to follow the lead

that has already been given by the government of the United States where the picture was similar in very many ways.
I am talking about co-operation and the joint investment in some of these great developments. As I have indicated, I shall leave the discussion of some of the particular projects in British Columbia and in the maritime provinces to the hon. members of our party from those provinces. Because I have spoken of this on a number of earlier occasions, and because my memory of this particular project goes back to my early boyhood, I do want to speak today about the project on the South Saskatchewan river and the reason why every hon. member of this house should be prepared to say now that we want action from this government in regard to the development of the South Saskatchewan river for power and for irrigation.
This subject has been before the house many times but this above all others is the time when encouragement should be given to the people of Saskatchewan and to the people of the prairie provinces by a definite decision on the part of this government that it will without any reservation proceed as *quickly as possible with the construction of the dam on the South Saskatchewan river which will provide both electricity and irrigation.
There need be no uncertainty in the mind of any hon. member as to the practical possibilities of this project. The skilled engineers under the P.F.R.A. have advocated that this be proceeded with. In order to have further and full support for the contention that this should be done the government appointed a royal commission. That royal commission made a finding which leaves no justification for any delay in a decision to proceed with the development. I would point out that, in spite of the immense scale of the development of the St. Lawrence river, the government did not feel impelled to appoint a royal commission to find out whether its engineers had been correct in their recommendations that it should proceed with the St. Lawrence river development. The government was prepared to rely on the advice of its own engineers and it did so with the full support of the hon. members of this house.
One cannot escape the thought that the appointing of a royal commission to deal with the various problems arising in connection with the South Saskatchewan river development was simply a delaying program and that it was not in fact done for the purpose of obtaining additional information. In any event, delay was pleaded as being justified on the ground that this commission had been
Power Development
appointed. That commission was appointed, it has reported, and its report has been available for a long time.
Granted that the figure, of course, is not small; granted that the figure, of course, may be difficult to determine down to the exact dollar some distance in advance. But, whether it be $135 million as originally estimated or $160 million as is now estimated, in any case there seems no uncertainty about the fact that the cost will be more than justified by the direct results and by the indirect results that would flow from this decision alone, even without waiting for the completion of that great project.
Near Outlook, in the province of Saskatchewan, there is visible proof of what can be done by irrigation in that very unfortunate area. Those who have been through that countryside know the desolate picture of abandoned homes, abandoned schools, abandoned churches and abandoned farms. Those who have been through that area know the difficulties under which those farmers have been carrying on for years, who have nevertheless carried on their farming activities. Throughout that whole great dry area of the Palliser triangle, the decision to go forward with the development of electricity and this great irrigation project would bring heart to people who have been discouraged and people who are doubly discouraged at this time with the problems of the failure of wheat marketing imposed on top of the difficulties they have already encountered. This great undertaking would change the whole aspect of that countryside. An area of 500,000 acres now under very limited production or no production at all would be irrigated. Those who have visited the experimental irrigation project near Outlook know that, with irrigation, that is rich, productive soil. In that experimental irrigation area, not only field crops but excellent root crops are being produced. Actually it is a garden area, and around it is grey, desolate, dry land.
It would be worth while to compare what is happening with what has happened not far away in North Dakota. Just across the boundary in North Dakota there was another power possibility. They have gone ahead in North Dakota with the construction of what is known as the Garrison dam. The comparative figures of those two projects are extremely interesting. It is true that the project in North Dakota is somewhat larger. Whereas in Saskatchewan 500,000 acres would be brought under cultivation by this irrigation, the Garrison dam project in North Dakota will irrigate 960,000 acres, just less than twice as much. Instead of 250,000 kilowatts of power produced by the dam on the South

Power Development
Saskatchewan, the Garrison dam project will produce 400,000 kilowatts, substantially less than twice as much. But let us see the comparative costs. The Garrison dam project, which will produce substantially less than twice as much, both in irrigation and in power, as will the South Saskatchewan river development, will cost $400 million, whereas the highest estimate that has been placed on the cost of the South Saskatchewan project is $160 million. All the economics are in favour of the project across the border on our side, in Saskatchewan. The engineers tell us it is practicable. The people of that area need the power and they need the irrigation, and the whole of the prairie provinces need the encouragement which would come from that great development.
Now let me just give you some of the figures of what it is estimated will come to North Dakota as a result of the Garrison dam project, which is considerably less than twice the project in South Saskatchewan. These are the figures of what they expect will come to North Dakota, as a minimum estimate, within the next ten years: 3,600 new farms; 1,700 new businesses; 20,000 new jobs; 93,000 more people, supported by the activities which will result from that development; and $250 million a year in new farm and business income. If the figures were comparable for Saskatchewan, then we would have well in excess of $125 million a year in new return from business and agricultural development that would come directly from that project, as against the initial cost of a maximum of $160 million for the completion of this project.
What is perhaps even more important is that, a result of the irrigation in North Dakota of 960,000 acres, the engineers who have advised on this project, which has now been positively undertaken, believe that this will stabilize the whole agricultural production of 18 million acres of agricultural land throughout the state. It is in that light that I think all of us should examine the possibilities of this great development. It is not only the 500,000 acres that would be directly irrigated; it is not only the elevation of spirit that would come from the sight of these new green acres that would emerge from the development of this project; it is the fact that the new agricultural activity and the secondary industries that would flow from the creation of power would stabilize the whole agricultural picture throughout Saskatchewan in a very large measure, at a time when every hon. member in this house has reason to recall from recent discussions that stabilization in that area is very greatly needed. There can be no reason of any kind to question the fact that we
[Mr. Drew.l
would gain even more substantially in Saskatchewan, in central eastern Alberta and throughout the whole prairie provinces by undertaking this project. What are the reasons for delay? What reasons have been given? The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who is prolific in statements that need correction afterwards, has given his explanation of why it is not being proceeded with. As reported in the Regina Leader-Post, and as stated already in the house, the Minister of Agriculture said:
We have been doing all right at clearing obstructions out of the way. There were four when we started discussions, and there is now only one left-the question of power development costs-
Let us hope that in this case he was accurate. After his lesson to the Liberal meeting here in Ottawa in January that you should not care too much about whether you believed in what you said as long as you said it with sufficient emphasis in support of the party line, perhaps it would not be inappropriate to wonder whether he believed what he was saying in this case. At any rate, there is his statement, that there was-

I am sure my hon. friend
will expect me to correct that one. I did not make any such statement at the Liberal meeting and no one has even reported that I did.

was giving them advice on how they should act and he recalled how, when he was in the cabinet of Mr. Mackenzie King, he had argued vigorously against a particular project in which he did not believe and when he went into the house he got up and made such a splendid advocacy of that particular project that as he was coming out someone said to him on the way out the door, "What could you have done, Jimmy, if you only believed in it?" speechtext:
It was a lesson which I
am sure the leader of a great party in this country often gives, namely, that no one person can be responsible for the setting up of policies for a great party, and I do not presume to do that for the Liberal party. I put forth my arguments in favour of what I think they ought to do, but when I am weighed down by the arguments of 20 others that it is not the right thing to do I get right into the team and go to work.

If you do that you should

I am quite prepared to let the record of what has been said here today

stand for itself in that regard. I would point out that, as the Minister of Agriculture has correctly pointed out, I have emphasized on many occasions that a minister of the crown has no right to speak on behalf of himself alone, and therefore I trust he was not speaking on behalf of himself alone when he said:
We have been doing all right at clearing obstructions out of the way. There were four when we started discussions, and there is now only one left-the question of power development costs.
They know the cost of power development, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: Since the Leader of the Opposition is reading the record he might read the remainder of the record in Hansard, the letter itself which was drafted by the government and sent to the government of Saskatchewan. That covers all the points in question.

subtopic: PARTICIPATION BY FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
I will follow with what I said immediately after my quotation the last time. I said:	"Mr. Chairman, some of us will
remember that Scotch song, 'Last night there were four Marys, tonight there are but three.' " In this case he only had one Mary still left and that was power production costs. This government has had the power production costs for a long time. They have the report of their own engineers. If they do not believe in their own engineers then they should do something about it. I am satisfied they have every reason to believe in the accuracy, skill and reliability of their own engineers who reported on this project, who said it should be proceeded with and who have given the power production costs. If that statement is a statement which accurately interprets the position of the government, then this project should have been proceeded with long ago. It should have been announced as a definite project of the government in the speech from the throne this year.
The farmers of western Canada need all the encouragement they can get at this time, particularly the farmers of central Saskatchewan whose problems are the greatest of all in this particular area that would be most closely associated with the development to which I have referred. If any evidence were needed of the fact that the government has been in power far too long, it is the way in which they continue to disregard the assurances given that this project would be proceeded with when they had the appropriate facts. If there is one thing needed to demonstrate beyond all question that this government has been in power too long and is unresponsive to the demands of those who feel that something should be done, it is that they would go ahead so quickly with projects elsewhere in the country and leave
Power Development
untouched a project which they have been dealing with for so long and in regard to which there have been so many generous assurances by the Minister of Agriculture.
If this development were proceeded with there would be challenging and inspiring new developments at Outlook and at other parts of the province of Saskatchewan. Everyone who has had anything to do with the production of electrical energy knows that if there is a firm core of substantial electric production from a hydroelectric source this is fed out into the transmission lines and makes it possible to maintain peak loads at distant points by auxiliary supply from diesel and thermo production in a way that would give an economic level of electricity cost throughout the whole area.
If the project is proceeded with, first of all there will be a use of part of the electricity for the pumping equipment of the irrigation project. There will be power employed by secondary industries that will start up in the area, and there will be further power available to flow out into the transmission lines throughout the province and make it possible at economic levels to carry low cost electricity to many distant points in the province of Saskatchewan.
Very recently a most imaginative plan was put forward in Regina with respect to the planned development of Outlook itself in relation to this project. It is the kind of thing that indicates what imagination, spirit and confidence could do in that area. This plan, put forward after examination by competent engineers and businessmen, recommended that there should be a planned program of development at Outlook, that secondary production should be encouraged to locate there, and that in addition to the new agricultural development that would come in that area a community should be planned of 10,000 or 11,000 people which would be an example to the whole of Saskatchewan and to other parts of the prairie provinces of what can be done by the use of resources of that kind.

I can assure hon. members of this house that any member of parliament, with a pass, should during his first term make up his mind that he is going to see this wonderful country in which we live-that sounds like a platitude, as it is said so often, but I really mean it sincerely-and to understand the great possibilities that are here, the great possibilities that I am convinced our grandchildren, those of us who have grandchildren, will see brought to fruition for the building up of this great country and for the benefit of the people who live therein.
The same thing applies to the maritimes. Last year I saw something my hon. friend from Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) has advocated for the whole time he has been here. In fact, I think that causeway joining Cape Breton to the mainland of Nova Scotia might have been christened the Gillis causeway. What a wonderful project that was! It may be that other projects along the coast of Nova Scotia will be undertaken sooner or later to the benefit not only of Nova Scotia but of all parts of Canada.
I quite agree with the Leader of the Opposition that, whilst some of these resources seem a long way from our centres of population, like the Grand falls he mentioned on the Hamilton river, today, with new methods of transmission, that power can be economically transmitted. I remember when we were discussing the Shipshaw project in this house, a project which I always thought was a remarkable engineering project though I had some criticisms of the manner in which it was financed at the time-but let that pass. I said at that time it was one of the most remarkable pieces of engineering not only in North America but in the world, and Canadian engineers were to be congratulated on having had the imagination to build that great dam and power plant. At that time it was said that when the war was ended the vast power that was being generated could not be transmitted far enough to keep that plant going as an economical unit. Well, it was transmitted and is being transmitted because from time to time, when the necessity has arisen, the inventive genius of man has been able to overcome difficulties of that description.
I come back now to my own province. I happen, of course, to be the member of parliament for the district in which Outlook is situated and the area of Saskatchewan that would benefit most from the building of that South Saskatchewan river dam. Of course, I think the Leader of the Opposition went a little far this afternoon when he described the area around where the dam
site would be, just below Outlook, as desolate and unproductive. As a matter of fact, I drove over it in the last week in July, and I had never seen anywhere a finer stand of wheat than I saw in that area. As the Leader of the Opposition said, the soil is productive if we can only get the water and, as there were copious rains last summer, there was a wonderful crop promising in that area. I use the word "promising" because over the centre of that whole area around Strongfield and right through to Davidson there was a devastating hail storm in the first week in August, and there was 100 per cent damage in that area to one of the finest stands of wheat I saw in Saskatchewan last summer. That soil is productive only when there is a rainfall. I was the member, not exactly for that area- because the boundaries of my constituency have been enlarged on the side of the river to which I have just referred-during the drought period, and I remember what the countryside looked like then. It looked like a desert, as a result of wind erosion. It was unproductive because it lacked water. I remember driving over a farm either in 1937 or the summer of 1938-it was probably 1937-with a gentleman who is now minister of highways in the province of Saskatchewan. We passed over an area of land that had been so wind-eroded that my friend said to me, "here is a piece of land that I believe will never produce another crop." I have seen some excellent crops on that very piece of land since, as I have driven by it, because we have had rain.
The government and some people in Canada may be lulled because we have had good crops in the Palliser triangle for several years past. We have had a period of unusually heavy rainfall over an unusual number of years. I do not think there is any doubt about that. But the day will come when we shall have, as we have had before, years of unusual drought when very little will grow. I use the words "very little" because I think our people in that area lacked much during the years of drought and depression and that there are newer and more efficient methods of production which may to some extent minimize a condition of that sort. But such conditions will occur again, and when they do, in spite of P.F.A.A. payments and all the rest of it-that is, the contributions made by the farmers into that fund-, if water is not available for irrigation, then it will cost this country again a tremendous amount of money to make up the deficiencies in the P.F.A.A. or-as I think is more likely -to give more relief than P.F.A.A. can give to the rural people in that area.

With regard to that dam, my understanding of the situation is that the Minister of Agriculture has gone to the province of Saskatchewan on several occasions, and each time the provincial government has either come close or has accepted the proposals he has made. At no time, however, did the Minister of Agriculture have cabinet approval for the plans he placed before that government. Bit by bit, the Saskatchewan government increased the amounts of money it was prepared to put into that plan, until, if my memory serves me correctly-and I am speaking from memory-the last time they agreed they would be prepared to accept a plan in the neighbourhood of $70 million and that they would undertake the electrical end of this project-a very important end, but not nearly as important as the other end, the irrigation side of it.
After the Leader of the Opposition had begun his address this afternoon, I sent up to my office for Hansard of February 21, 1938. I had been in the house two years at that time and I had spoken on the Saskatchewan river on the estimates of the department. Then on February 21, 1938, I moved the following resolution:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should place before parliament at an early date plans, or proposals, for a comprehensive and authoritative survey of water conservation, irrigation possibilities and other feasible projects for the permanent rehabilitation of the drought stricken area of western Canada and its people.
That is not so far removed from the sort of proposal that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) has put before us this afternoon. When I moved that resolution, Mr. Speaker, I had preceded it with a good deal of investigation. I had made up my mind from what I had learned that the South Saskatchewan river project was a feasible project. I had been to two of our universities and had met outstanding university people who had made some study of such projects. They had convinced me that the proposal was feasible, sound and economic.
I had also gone to the library of parliament and there read the Palliser report and the Hind report, to which very few people ever refer, on the conditions that those two early explorers had found in western Canada in the mid-fifties. I quoted voluminously from them. I am not going to quote from these reports this afternoon. I merely refer to them and say to hon. members who are really interested in this subject: Go to the library, take a look at these reports and see what the condition was in that country in the 1850's or in the 1880's. I am referring particularly to the 1850's, and it is evident that 100 years ago there were many years of drought. Think
Power Development
of what may happen again within a measurable period of time, particularly in view of our demands upon the soil for chemicals and moisture for the production of grain. We may find ourselves faced with a condition of this sort sooner than we think.
I remember that I recounted how a friend of mine had been standing on the banks of the South Saskatchewan that very summer and had noted the vast quantities of water flowing through the parched lands. Although the same is not equally true, it is true to some extent of the North Saskatchewan river. I went on to say, as found at page 638 of Hansard of February 21, 1938:
X have gone carefully over the contour maps of the dried-out area, and as a layman I would say that wide-scale irrigation seems to present no insuperable difficulties, either physical or financial, on the northern side of the Missouri-Coteau divide.
At that time, Mr. Speaker, not only did I believe that irrigation was desirable and feasible but that electrical projects were feasible too. I should like to quote from page 639 where I had this to say:
The valleys of both the Saskatchewan rivers lie between great banks and there are several places where dams could be conveniently located and power generated if desired.
I went on to refer by inference to the old Pearce proposals of the early part of this century and said:
If it were necessary to divert some water from the North to the South Saskatchewan river, and to supplement the latter, irrigating the intervening county as it flowed, I believe that could be done.
So, Mr. Speaker, this matter has been before us for years and had been before the house years before I came here. I placed it before the house on February 21, 1938, just 18 years ago tomorrow. I went on to say:
I have been told by engineers that dams placed at intervals on the South Saskatchewan, south of Saskatoon, to the point at which the Red Deer joins the South Saskatchewan in Alberta, would Impound sufficient water to give moisture to the whole of central and southeastern Saskatchewan. I do not know. But that is something we should, as a parliament, find out. The little sloughs and large lakes now dry could be filled, and the table level of subsoil moisture raised again to its old level, while in many years an inch or two of water on the parched land at the right time would ensure a bountiful return for the labour expended.
Whether or not southeastern Saskatchewan could be irrigated, I do not know, but when I examined these contour maps in the hands of a competent hydraulic engineer, to whom I was recommended by some of the people at McGill University, he indicated that it could be done. But undoubtedly between 400,000 and 500,000 acres in my constituency could be irrigated. Undoubtedly the demonstration carried on by the Minister of Agriculture and his department at Outlook demonstrated very

Power Development
clearly the productivity of the soil. As I have indicated, however, you do not need such a demonstration because if there is plenty of rainfall in that area the soil has been shown to be productive, although what the Department of Agriculture has done is to show that crops could be diversified.
The town of Outlook, situated as it is in a strategic position to take advantage of these irrigation and power projects, could be expanded. I should like to say this further word. We were talking a few minutes ago of transmitting power from some of the great power plants at the coal mines or rivers to the centres of population. I think there is a more important thought, the thought of building up places like Outlook and the many other "Outlooks", if I may call them such, across Canada so that we may diversify our production, so that we may move it away from these great centres of population where there is overcrowding and where, in the event of war, I do not see how the civil defence organization could operate effectively. I do not see how the civil defence organization could, for example, evacuate the city of Montreal, the city of Toronto, even the city of Ottawa or the other major cities across Canada. I am not thinking that we are going to have a nuclear war but in the interests of health, in the interests of building communities with a community spirit where individuals in the community may know one another, the more of these relatively smaller cities we can establish the better it will be for our country in the final analysis.
I am very glad to rise this afternoon and support the amendment. If I were moving an amendment to it I think I might emphasize the South Saskatchewan river project. However, the Leader of the Opposition emphasized that sufficiently in his address. I do not know whether my colleagues will be content, because I have not had a chance to talk to them, but I am going to content myself with supporting the amendment moved and recommending to the government not only the project in which I am particularly interested because I represent the people who inhabit that area but also that a very thorough survey be undertaken with the provincial governments so that there may be a joint development of some of these great projects in the maritimes, in western Canada and in other parts of this great country.
One only has to travel in the northern part of Canada to realize what tremendous resources there are available. I have been told by people who know something about what is going on in our own northland and what has been going on in Siberia and the Arctic regions of Russia that we are 20 or

30 years behind the Soviet union in developing our northern resources and that we should be paying much more attention to the great resources we have in that north country.
Bear in mind the fact that it would not require any joint agreement with any province. These northern resources are in the northwest territories of Canada under the control of this parliament. If the government is unwilling to enter into arrangements with the provinces to develop some of these resources, then let the. government do more to develop that great north land. Perchance, now that the iron curtain is being lifted a little bit-and I hope it will be lifted some more-we might be able to get some data on how to deal, for example, with permafrost and some of the other problems that exist in the north country, as the result of the experiments that have been carried out in Siberia and in the northern reaches of Russia.
I want to join the Leader of the Opposition in recommending to the government the consideration of this report. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that is the only way in which I wish to join him.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. G. J. Hahn (New Westminster):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are indeed pleased to have the privilege of going along with this motion. In speaking to it I may say that our group is wholeheartedly in support thereof. I was greatly interested in some of the remarks which the leader of the official opposition had to make, more particularly the statement to the effect that if the party of which I am a member have a political philosophy they had more fortune than anyone else.
I may assure him that we have a political philosophy. The fact is that it has proven to be so good that we have never had to look back. We are one of the few political parties that are not looking back. We are the only political group that has increased the number of governments we have in this country at this time.
He also brought in the word "secession". To my knowledge I do not believe any member of this group during the course of the past few days, when we were discussing the question of wheat, brought that word into the debate. Reference undoubtedly was made to what the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Johnson) had to say. I would agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) who indicated that over a period of years the word has been quite frequently used in the west.
Hon. members are probably aware of the fact that I spent much of my early life in Saskatchewan and Alberta and only in recent years became a citizen of British Columbia.

During that time it was not an uncommon thing to hear the word "secession" in the dried out sections in the southwestern corner of the province of Saskatchewan in around Hatton, Maple Creek, Piapot and that area with which I am so familiar, and then carrying on into the city of Medicine Hat. However, I do not believe anyone was really and truly in earnest. It was just an emotional feeling that they were not being looked after with the proper attention. I would say that they used it more for the purpose of directing the attention of the government to that particular problem than with the intention of putting it into effect.
I am satisfied that the people of the far west-and certainly this is so in my own province-would be much opposed to the thought of secession at this time or at any other time. We joined to make the Dominion of Canada a stronger and better place in which to live as a group, not a place in which we might get what we alone desire. However, we expect our fair share, and that is where the rub comes in.
Frequently I have heard constituents of mine and others as well-and I have possibly made a similar observation-say that the governmental friends, the Liberals as a whole, are a fine bunch of fellows taken as individuals but that they hatch some of the worst legislation this country has seen. I did not use the word "worst"; I used a stronger term. In the far west and particularly in British Columbia it seems to us at this time that the legislation is not meant to call for unity in Canada but rather for more of what the leader of the official opposition had to say in respect thereto, namely that it is localized too much in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec and that fact causes a great deal of dissension.
In the course of his discussion the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar drew attention to the fact that in Saskatchewan there was apparently a Conservative who received both the Liberal nomination and the Conservative nomination, and who is going to run under that banner in this coming election. I should like to remind hon. members and all Canadians as a whole that this is not an uncommon thing in the far west, more particularly in British Columbia. We had there an alliance between the C.C.F. and the Liberals in a good number of cases. In Alberta in the last provincial election they not only had a Liberal-C.C.F. member but they had a C.C.F.-Liberal-Conservative, whatever that is. They did not have just one; they had several of them. They were endorsed by each political party.
It reached this point. If the system of proportional representation proved nothing else,
Power Development
it definitely proved that there was a coalition between the C.C.F. and the Liberal party. In one of the provincial ridings within the Jasper-Edson area I am told that in the vote, of the 1,100 second choices that went from the C.C.F. member, 900 went to the Liberal candidate and 200 to the Social Credit candidate, even though the Social Credit candidate had a majority of over 200 on the first count. I am satisfied that would indicate to the hon. member from Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott), who likes to jeer at others, that he has run as a C.C.F'er, as an independent, as a Liberal.
I do not know whether the Conservatives would have him or not but we certainly did not and we do not intend to. But that should indicate to the people that there is apparently very little to choose between these people who would run under these numerous badges and call themselves particular groups; who can run as socialists or Conservatives and still be Liberals, as was indicated by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar.

speechtext:
I am coming to the resolution. I am just answering some of those things that were suggested earlier. It should not worry you because you realize full well that the things I am saying must be true. We did not coalesce with anyone when we had a minority government in British Columbia; it was not our intention to do so and it is not today nor will it be at any time.
The leader of the official opposition suggested that Canada was divided for political purposes. I do not think he has to repeat that for those in the west. The people in the prairie provinces, particularly west of Manitoba, frequently suggest that they have become the milk cow of Canada. We have heard that suggestion time and again in the past few days and in former debates. In the resolution proposed by the Leader of the Opposition there is much in common, with what we have suggested from time to time. His motion reads:
in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to a joint investment program for the development of power resources in any province where the government of such province requests the co-operation of the Canadian government in carrying out such development.
At pages 9 and 10 of the Social Credit manifesto, interestingly enough, we read this with respect to natural resources:
A Social Credit Canadian government would co-operate with the provincial governments in stimulating the opening up of new areas and fields for discovery and development of natural resources, with a view to establishing national policies of self-sufficiency in the essentials of living. Their general policy would be to encourage

Power Development
the development ot all those resources which can contribute to the economical production of goods within the country.
You see, while the terms are not identical, certainly the fact remains that we believe in complete co-operation, between federal and provincial authorities. I have tried to stress that from time to time, not only in connection with this matter but in connection with many others. It was my intention to bring to the attention of this house later the fact that there is not sufficient of this particular type of co-operation. Members on the government side seem to get the idea that because of the huge proportion of members on the government side, they can force anything upon those areas which are suffering in a particular fashion. Despite any representations that might be made, these areas are not being given the hearing they have every right to expect.
This just does not happen in one instance. It has happened in many instances. There is not sufficient co-ordination among the various departments, and I shall refer specifically to the Department of Transport and the Department of Public Works. I have mentioned this before. I see the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) looking at me. I have referred to a particular problem which exists in my area, but I shall refer to it in more detail at a later time because it is not relevant to this particular resolution. However, I would once again say most definitely that we are in complete agreement with this particular resolution, and for several reasons.
In British Columbia we have water power which has not been developed and we have a great need for that particular development. A year ago there was an extensive debate on a project known as the Kaiser dam in connection with the Columbia river development. We received a hearing and consideration from the committee, and we have abided by that consideration. But today we find that British Columbia is in great need of the development of some of its potential water power resources. We have industries that are anxious to come into our province. It is not an uncommon thing to hear that the lower mainland is running short of water power. There is a reason for it. We have an agreement with the northwestern states of the United States for the exchange of electrical energy. Our population has grown so rapidly and we have so many more industries in the area that today we have not sufficient water power developed in British Columbia to. look after our own needs.
For that reason we have had a thorough examination made of the water resources of the province. We find that through a diversion scheme on the Columbia river, such as

that referred to by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage), we could add approximately 20 million horsepower to our water power development. This, of course, would cost a tremendous sum. I am rather amused when I hear the leader of the C.C.F. suggest that we should not allow United States capital to come in and help us develop that power. Certainly we need that money. The important thing, so far as the people of British Columbia are concerned, is to see that there is work available. We cannot have work available unless we have water power developed within our province.
It might be said, why cannot the people of Canada finance that development? I am satisfied that you realize as well as I do, as do most of our socialist-minded friends, that you cannot build a huge dam for nothing; that is just wishful thinking. Some of these dams cost anywhere from $300 million to $750 million. It takes a great deal more capital than the Canadian public can afford to invest within the country for its proper development. We lack the capital for proper development.
It seems to me that, for that reason, we are going to have to make certain agreements which, at this time, may not appear to be to the advantage of Canada as a whole if viewed on the strictly Conservative basis of Canada first. I would suggest, therefore, that we must have closer co-operation and a better understanding between the federal government and the provinces, as is suggested in this resolution, for the purpose of developing everything we have in this country to the optimum. We speak of war with Russia or the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. We are not ready for it. No nation is ready for it unless it is working at full speed. Certain of our industries are in a depressed condition, and certain of them have been shut down because they have not sufficient power. We are trying to look after that problem in this section of Canada, I would agree to that.
I would agree to the development of any water power project in New Brunswick or any of the other provinces. Through our premier we have been battling with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) with respect to the development of the have-not areas. They cannot be expected to do anything unless they have the power and the means. Undoubtedly as a result of the development of this project that has been suggested in New Brunswick we will find that New Brunswick will prosper as well as the whole of the maritimes.
But that is not the answer to the problem of British Columbia. We have found it necessary to go out of British Columbia to obtain

capital for these developments. As a result of having to get that assistance from outside the area, we are being told by other citizens, particularly the socialists and those who believe in the Canada first policy, that we must develop Canada as a whole.
It is understandable that if Canadian funds are being utilized in Quebec and Ontario, as apparently they are, then it is going to be necessary for us to get some of that capital from other sources. In order to get that capital we must be prepared to give certain concessions. In British Columbia we have the Kitimat project, which will sustain a population of about 50,000 people. The diversion scheme on the Stikine and Liard rivers would take care of another 250,000 or 300,000, and the Frobisher project would add another 150,000. In other words, as a result of the proper development of these two diversion schemes we would be able to look after approximately another half million people in the northern part of our province.
In recent weeks we have had a proposal made that there should be a dam on the Fraser river, a project which is commonly known as the Moran dam. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair), and quite rightly so, objects to the whole scheme. I would agree with him. Any damming of the Fraser river that will affect our fishing industry in an adverse way should be opposed. We were going to develop the southern end of the Columbia river to begin with, the part crossing the border. We were denied that privilege. As a result the people of British Columbia have been denied the receipt of $2 million annually, which would be their share from that particular project. Foreign capital and Canadian capital have not been prepared to come in since and develop the upper part of the Columbia, by the Mica creek dam, which we were assured should be the first part to be developed. The Canadian government is not doing anything about it either.
I put a question to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources some time ago, and he said that up to that time there had been one request for a licence for a project which is already in operation. That is understandable. The people who have the capital to invest in industry and require power are not interested in investing it where we might suggest. They want to develop the project in a certain region and at a particular place, and they expect the right to do so if they are to invest their money. It is not being invested just for the purpose of doing Canadians a good turn.

A C.C.F. government was elected, but the property was not necessarily exploited. Those concerned did not go ahead and spend millions of dollars on drilling, with the possibility of drilling a dry hole and then having to turn it over to a government, in which most capitalists fear to invest. Today capital has a right to expect a fair return. I am satisfied that most hon. members will agree with me in that; and what is more, Canadians have indicated, in two provinces at least, that they agree with us. They are prepared to

Power Development
accept United States investment, British investment, or investment from any other country that we can interest to the extent of coming into this country, provided they come in under our regulations. We are in a position, if we wish to do so, to make laws in respect of any of this capital that might be coming in. I would say that the elected representatives in the provinces and in the federal government should be capable of looking after the interests of Canadians as a whole.
May I return to British Columbia electric power development. We have one major electrical firm in British Columbia known as British Columbia Electric. That company has realized for some time that there is a need for power development in that province. In an effort to have our power developed properly and in their desire to protect industry as well, which is most important, they have set aside the significant sum of $50,000 to discover a means by which salmon spawn can be taken up to the headwaters safely.
Some of our friends have already suggested that capital is not willing to invest money without exploiting the country. Here we have an industry which has been with us in British Columbia for a great many years. Besides the profit motive that the hon. gentleman suggests, this company has the interests of the people of British Columbia at heart, just as any other firm might have, or just as an individual might have; because if the people in our province failed they would have to leave, and if they leave the British Columbia Electric will have to leave, and they are no more interested in doing that than is anybody else. They have indicated their interest by suggesting that this money be made available to the University of British Columbia. The university in turn has asked Dr. Shrum, who is one of the great scientists in that province, to look after this particular project and see whether means can be found to have development in both ways.
I could speak on this subject of the Fraser river project for a long time. I have ten more minutes to go, but at the same time I realize that as many hon. members as possible would like to have the privilege of speaking on this question. I shall therefore give way to the next hon. member.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am craving the indulgence of the house while I deal with the amendment for a few moments, believing that it focuses attention on a new type of policy which is needed in this country. There have been policies that have been somewhat of the nature proposed by this amendment, but this goes quite a bit further, and I am hoping that the government will see fit to accept the amendment.

We all know that as Canada grows and new developments become possible the need arises to reassess governmental policies. The amendment here, I submit, Your Honour, deals with one field in which there is need for such reassessment. For the purpose of the record I read the pertinent part of the amendment which is that:
.. .consideration should be given to a joint investment program for the development of power resources in any province where the government of such province requests the co-operation of the Canadian government in carrying out such development.
You will notice that the method of participation is not set out. We have not attempted to go that far. I think the method is a matter to be worked out in each case, and it will perhaps differ in each case.
The dominion part in a joint program might be by way of a direct contribution, by way of a guarantee or by actually doing some of the work that is necessary in order that the project can be completed. I think the main thing is to make it possible for the credit of the dominion to be put behind the credit of the provinces where developments of the kind contemplated are to be undertaken. That is not necessary, of course, with the provinces of Ontario and Quebec because I understand they can finance on practically as favourable terms as the nation itself.
The main point we seek to drive home in this amendment is that there should be an acceptance of some responsibility by the federal government. Such a policy is needed particularly in the case of rivers flowing over the border into the United States. I say that because last year the government-and I agreed with the action-took a licensing control over the improvements on international rivers by means of a statute which was described as the International River Improvements Act.
The purpose of that act was really to provide for the licensing of international river improvements to ensure that the water resources of Canada are developed and utilized in the national interest. That control, while necessary, does restrict the provinces considerably, and it puts the federal government under some obligation to co-operate in at least a portion of any improvements of these river systems. Otherwise, were that not the case, the federal government would be in the position of a dog in the manger in so far as the development of these particular rivers is concerned. There has been no actual application made in respect of the Kaiser dam, but we all know that the attitude of the dominion government was that it would not permit the construction of that dam.

Now, it is not good enough for the dominion simply to say to a province, "No, you cannot go ahead with this scheme." I submit that the dominion must be prepared to take steps to help by offering some alternate scheme. The difficulty that arose on the Columbia river system last year was the situation which brought about the enactment of the International River Improvements Act. I should like to review for a moment or two the facts with regard to the Columbia river system.
It is a great power river, third in importance on the North American continent, surpassed only by the Mississippi and the St. Lawrence; and I believe that it is of about the same importance as the St. Lawrence river system. Three-fifths of the power that can be developed on that river system is in the United States. That is, it can be developed by use of the Columbia river where it is flowing within the United States boundaries. One-fifth can be developed wholly within Canada and the remaining one-fifth can only be developed by storage of water in Canada for use in United States power plants below the boundary.
The dominion and the province of British Columbia have been making joint surveys for many years having in mind the proper development of this river system in Canada. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources can correct me if I am wrong, but I think the international joint commission has been investigating conditions on this particular river for ten or eleven years.
At the moment one of the great questions which remains unsettled as between Canada and the United States is whether there will be any payment for what is known as downstream benefits; whether, for example, the United States will pay anything to Canada for the storage of water in Canada which is to be used subsequently on the United States side of the line. That question is unsettled.
To this picture we add the Kaiser deal of a year or 18 months ago. Then the act follows which was passed last year, and since ther; there appears to have been a stalemate develop. I can only plead today as I did last session for co-operation between the two governments, the federal government and the government of the province of British Columbia. This question will never be settled satisfactorily unless there is such co-operation.
I was somewhat disturbed to hear the remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for New Westminster, because he indicated that he was in favour of United States development of the Columbia river
67509-86J
Power Development
system in Canada. That is the stand taken just two weeks ago by the minister of lands and forests in the British Columbia legislature. I refer to Hon. Mr. Sommers. I have in my hand a press dispatch of his speech, and among other remarks he had these words to say; I am quoting from the Vancouver Province of February 7:
He made it clear the government will still deal with the U.S. for development of a big power and storage dam at Mica creek, high in the Columbia river system.
The Mica creek development is the main development on the Columbia river system in Canada. Conditions are such that that development could be proceeded with in the very near future and here is a provincial minister, the minister in charge of this particular type of work in British Columbia, making this statement. The dispatch continues:
Mr. Sommers accused members of the federal government of "an appalling act of irresponsibility", and several times described Liberal leader Arthur Laing as the Liberal party's "chief apologist in B.C."
He said the B.C. government's policy for the Columbia is to have the Mica creek dam "built free of cost to the people of B.C.; that we have the control and generation of all at-site power for the use of B.C., and that we would expect delivery of 20 per cent of the gross power generated (additional) on the American side by this storage, delivered cost-free to the province of B.C."
No better plan has been devised, he said.
He declined to specify whether American public or private money would build the storage dam.
What better deal could there be. he demanded. Besides getting the dam free, B.C. would get all the power generated at the dam and 20 per cent of the power the same water-once it had reached the American side-would generate in American hydro plants.
If that policy is put into effect it means that the Puget Sound utilities council will be doing that development. The Puget Sound utilities council is made up of the Puget Sound Power and Light Company, which is a private company operating in the state of Washington; Seattle City Light, a municipal system; Tacoma City Light, another municipal system; Snohomish county public utility district and Chelan public utility district, both of which are public utility districts. Those five power organizations make rather a queer combination, but they have combined into the Puget Sound utilities council, and it is hoped that they would be in partnership with the United States federal government in many of the projects. Possibly the Mica creek project would be one in which the Puget Sound utilities council would be doing the work, with the backing of United States federal government money or of the credit of the United States government.
That, of course, is directly opposed to the plan for the development of the Columbia river system envisaged by General

Power Development
McNaughton. He, of course, is in favour of this Mica creek development at the earliest possible time. He has advocated a series of other dams, which I need not enumerate today. He has dealt with the question of downstream benefits, and also suggested that it might be possible to divert the headwaters of the Kootenay river into the Columbia river system and allow a portion of the Columbia river water into the Fraser river system. I am not taking a position today either for or against these diversions. There is a great deal of controversy in British Columbia as to whether or not General McNaughton is correct in advocating those two diversions, but his whole plan is to have this work done by Canadians for Canadians.
There we have a direct conflict between the two plans. Apparently the dominion government and the British Columbia government are again at loggerheads over the development of this system. Unfortunately, time is an element in this question. Canada cannot afford to sit back and wait for something to develop. The problem is very pressing. Yet there is no indication whatever that the federal government is moving to meet this situation. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources should give this house a statement during this debate as to what the dominion proposes to do with regard to this question.
Clearly, here on the Columbia river system there is a case for a joint investment program by the two governments. If such a program were adopted the result would be to keep control of the system in Canada. There would be a great saving if the federal government put its credit behind any such development. The plans could be proceeded with much more quickly, and that means that the people in British Columbia would have cheaper power at an earlier date, with resulting benefits throughout the whole economy of that part of Canada. There would be new industries.
This development of the Columbia river system would be the greatest development that has ever taken place in British Columbia. There has never been anything there of this magnitude. It would mean an expansion of towns and an increase in population. Once the whole plan becomes actually effective, I believe the result will be an increase of a million people in the province of British Columbia, and there would be so many more people to consume the wheat that is grown on the prairies, which is giving us so much trouble at the present time. For that reason alone my suggestions to the government today should be acceptable, for then they would not hear so much about wheat in

future sessions. It would mean increased strength for the nation as a whole.
I point out that there would be very little risk to the dominion in entering into a joint investment program of this kind. These works, I believe, would be self-liquidating. It is merely a matter of the dominion putting its credit behind the province. Just a few months ago we had a great talk about joint investment programs. When the dominion-provincial conference met in April of last year one of the four subjects set over for consideration in the fall was as follows:
Public investment and natural resources development.
Under that heading this particular scheme certainly should come. The province of British Columbia sent representatives here in October, and the premier of that province had this to say in his brief. I am quoting from page 5, under the heading "Public Investment":
British Columbia submits that the federal government should participate jointly with the provinces in investment in capital projects directed to the expansion of the productive wealth of Canada. Such public investment is a capital expenditure warranted by the return which will accrue both to the nation and to the province.
In giving the details of his plans he did not mention the development of power. But I suggest that he be taken at his word, and that the dominion say, "We are prepared to go into a joint program of this kind for the development of the Columbia river power." I submit that with regard to this particular river-and I point out that next to the St. Lawrence it is the most important one in Canada so far as power is concerned-we are at a fork in the road. One way will lead to great expansion by Canadians for Canadians, and I believe that way would be by a joint investment program. The other way we shall have expansion in Canada by Americans, primarily for Americans-make no mistake about that-with Canadians losing partial control and getting only partial benefits. I do not believe there are very many in this house who wish to see a policy adopted which leads to that second result.
It is obvious that the province of British Columbia cannot do this development itself, particularly under the curb of the dominion licensing control which exists under the International River Improvements Act. It is absolutely necessary that there be a partnership. If a joint program can be worked out, nothing would do more to help the Canadians who live on the Pacific slope. I would like to see more co-operative suggestion coming from the west coast, but I hope the dominion government will make an offer to the province of British Columbia to hold discussions. Why

should the two governments remain at arm's length and snarling at each other across 3,000 miles of Canada? Their representatives should be meeting to discuss this question.
With regard to downstream benefits, the Canadian government should be meeting with the United States government, and I see no reason why the government of British Columbia should not have representatives sitting in on those discussions. In some parts of the country, for the orderly development of power by Canadians we must have a joint investment policy.
As I said in my opening remarks, I place these thoughts before the house today, and particularly before the government, in the hope that the policy outlined in this amendment will be accepted. This amendment is not brought forward simply to make trouble for the government. It is brought forward in the belief that a policy of this kind should be adopted by Canada, and I hope it will be possible for the government to treat the amendment in that way.

I think the fairest presentation of the whole power situation in the upper Columbia region was made by United States Senator Richard L. 1.	Insistence on maximum development.-The value of the vast hydroelectric power potential lying dormant in the river canyons of British Columbia is well understood north of the border. The people of the province and their representatives have seen the progress which 20 years of Columbia river development in the United States have brought to the Pacific northwest. They visualize an industrial empire for western Canada, built on the full utilization of the water power latent in their portion of the Columbia river basin.
2.	Canadian resources for Canada.-Canadians generally would prefer this full utilization to benefit the industrial development of their own Pacific northwest and are averse to the direct or indirect "export" of their water power potential to the more developed power market of the United States. Their convictions in this respect reflect both national pride and a confident long-range view of the future of western Canada.
3.	Recognition of public responsibility.-Both in public meetings and in private conversations the view was repeatedly expressed that only the national governments of Canada and the United States can work out a settled program for mutually beneficial upstream development and downstream benefits in the Columbia river basin; and that the dominion and the provincial government in British Columbia, acting in continuing co-operation with the United States government, can best undertake developments of the magnitude of those possible on the upper Columbia river.
