I am talking about the situation that was raised with respect to the development of water resources in British Columbia. Like the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra, as a British Columbia member and as one who resides in the district and represents a large area in the district, I am particularly interested in the development of the Columbia basin. I have been interested in that matter for a good many years, even prior to the reference of 1944. Since that time I suppose 95 per cent of the investigation of the Columbia river basin has been carried on at the expense of the federal government, and rightly so.
At this point I must pay a tribute to the good work of the officials of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and the Department of Public Works who have been doing that work throughout the basin since 1945. I am sure it will not be many months until we shall have some idea of the result and some conclusions drawn from that long-term investigation.
Last session the discussion on the international rivers bill in the house, and also in the committee hearing the evidence given by witnesses, created a great deal of interest and a much wider understanding of this question so far as the Columbia river is concerned. Since that time, as mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver South, we had a visit by Senator Richard L. Neuberger of Oregon. He is a member of the interior and insular affairs committee of the United States Senate. I know Senator Neuberger quite well and was pleased to make certain arrangements for him. I arranged for him to meet certain organizations and to address certain meetings. I made travel arrangements and provided him with the opportunity of examining the situation, and of meeting organizations and people in the district in order to secure material for writing what I think is an excellent report to his committee in the United States Senate.
I am not saying that I agree with all his conclusions, but at least from the Canadian point of view it was written very fairly indeed. He had an opportunity to address a number of public bodies such as city councils, boards of trade, chambers of commerce, committees and other small meetings, and he obtained a fairly good idea of the thinking of the people in the district. He was

Power Development
greatly impressed by the concern of Canadians he met in the area and in British Columbia generally about the development of this basin, that it should be developed to the advantage of Canadians and that Canadian rights and interests should be protected.
In any event, he was greatly interested in the widespread interest in the question and to what an extent a large section of the public was quite generally informed on it. In addition, in his report he mentioned one significant thing. He said that, although generally speaking all parties he met were suggesting the necessity for the development as the result of the investment of public funds, nowhere did he hear the word "socialism" referred to. He was quite taken with the fact that all parties he met supported these proposals and no one suggested that this was a form of socialism. His visit, I think, was fruitful from the American and the Canadian point of view. His visit was largely the result of United States concern over proposals being made in Canada for the diversion of the Columbia river into the Fraser river.
I want to draw the particular attention of the house to a series of articles written by Mr. Grant Dexter in the Winnipeg Free Press of November 12, 14 and 15. I suggest that anybody who is interested in this question should read those articles, because Mr. Grant Dexter has clearly grasped the core of this whole situation. I think the articles are well worth reading by anyone who is interested in understanding the position of the Canadian section of the international joint commission and the position of this government with respect to this proposed development.
Mr. Dexter is one of an increasing number who recognize the splendid efforts that General McNaughton is making to see, so far as he and the commission are concerned, that these developments do take place to the full advantage of the Canadian people.
Now, I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South. I do not think we can come to definite conclusions. We must have all the facts before us before we can start to draw conclusions. I am sure that those members of the house who are interested in this subject are awaiting with interest the report on the investigation that is being made into the possibility of the diversion of the Columbia into the Fraser. When we have that report on the investigation from the commission, we will be in a position to analyse the situation and know to a greater extent what we are talking about.
This development is of some importance to the Kootenay country generally. It is of particular importance because, as the member

for Vancouver-Quadra said, there is a possibility for the development of this power in relation to the great natural resources that exist in the area. I think everyone in this house will recall that members on the government side speaking on this subject last year, and General McNaughton in the committee, laid particular stress upon the fact that every recognition was given to the rights of the province in regard to the development of natural resources and that these developments come directly within provincial jurisdiction. Therefore, after we get the report there is no question about it but that one would expect the provincial governments, like the rest, to study them and make certain proposals.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra dealt with certain proposals made recently by the minister of lands and forests in the legislature of British Columbia. I have a transscript of that speech, and I shall just read from it briefly. The minister says:
Our policy in respect to the Mica development is:
X. That we expect to have the storage dam built free of cost to the people of British Columbia.
2.	That we would have the control and generation of all at-site power for the use of British Columbia.
3.	That we would expect delivery of 20 per cent of the gross power generated on the American side by this storage, delivered cost free to the province of British Columbia.
I presume that is the policy of the government of British Columbia with respect to the development at Mica creek at this time. I believe that would clearly indicate they are looking forward to United States capital building this dam.
I am concerned directly because of my interest in this question, but the particular reason I have for supporting this resolution, in addition to its general importance, is the fact that it points to a joint public investment program for the development of our power resources. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra I thought very well said, one method means United States capital and with it a measure of United States control and profits. The other way means using our national credit, based on Canadian natural resources, to develop Canadian natural resources to the advantage of Canadians generally. I believe, Mr. Speaker that if this could be done then a spirit of co-operation would exist among all governments.

This is a very interesting resolution that we have before us, Mr. Speaker. We have heard of the great interest and benefit it would be to western Canada in the development of the South Saskatchewan and Columbia rivers, as

well as other rivers in the west. I do not suppose there is any part of Canada which would rejoice more if the government would adopt this motion than the maritime provinces. I myself am very pleased indeed that the matter has been brought before the house, and I sincerely hope it will receive the en-dorsation of this parliament.
The idea is not new at all. The hon. member who just took his seat stated he thought his party had introduced it first in this house. I do not know about that, nor do I think it makes very much difference. But I know that the idea has been prevalent in my own province for quite a number of years. The present premier of New Brunswick, at a recent meeting of the provincial premiers with the federal government, brought the matter to the attention of that conference.
I should like to read, Mr. Speaker, from a speech that was made by the premier of New Brunswick in the provincial house at Fredericton last year. He said:
The federal government proposed for consideration two subjects:-*
This was at the dominion-provincial conference.
-taxation and unemployment. Right here is Where the New Brunswick delegation differed. We went to Ottawa primarily to stress the opposite of unemployment, namely employment. The first item on our agenda was, and I quote-
Premier Flemming is quoting from his own agenda.
"Our first proposal is that an important place on the agenda should be accorded to the principle of the federal financial assistance to the provinces for the broad purpose of resource development.
He went on to say that he was thinking of Beechwood and other hydro developments in the province of New Brunswick.
As I say, the idea is not new so far as this house is concerned. I recall that quite a few years ago there was the development of the Tennessee Valley Authority in the United States. This great development was brought about' by the federal government for the benefit of the southern states, which were not receiving the attention they should. There was not the industry in that part of the country, and it was felt that what was necessary was some great hydro development.
After the development of the Tennessee valley power, industry did flow to that section of the country. This was true not only of the Tennessee valley project but it was true also of the great northwestern section of the United States. The same idea has been advanced by the commonwealth countries in the Colombo plan. We speak about the necessity for the development of hydroelectric
Power Development
power in India, and we claim also that it is our privilege to assist in that development in Egypt and Ceylon.
Here I should like to state that in my opinion, if such a development is good for different sections of the United States, if it is proper that we as Canadian members of the commonwealth should assist in this development in countries like India, China-perhaps I should not mention China-India, Ceylon and Egypt, then surely it is right that we should do everything possible to develop every section of our own country.
I do not think that in the whole of Canada there is greater need for hydro development than there is in the maritime provinces today. This subject has been discussed in this house on numerous occasions. I myself have pointed out the great dearth of electric power in my own province of New Brunswick. I understand that the average amount of electric power in Ontario and Quebec is one horsepower per capita. In New Brunswick we have a population of about 500,000 people. Our hydro electric development amounts to 136,000 horsepower. Anyone can see the great difference between hydro development in New Brunswick-and the same applies to Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island-and in the central provinces, and even in the province of British Columbia. We did not feel this lack of development so much until recent years.
In the last two or three years we have discovered great mineral wealth in our province. We hope to develop the minerals of our own province; we hope that smelters will be built in the northern part of New Brunswick so that minerals produced there will not be shipped away to be smelted in other parts of the world, as is being done at the present time. That is the hope of every citizen of New Brunswick, and it has been expressed at different times. Today there is the prospect of further development of our pulp and paper industry.
I might say in that connection, Mr. Speaker, for years the province of New Brunswick has been shipping out of the province anywhere from 500,000 to nearly 1 million cords of pulp-wood. We want to process and develop that in New Brunswick. The only way it can be done and will be done is to produce cheap electric power in the province. Today there is talk of a mill being built on the south shore of the province, on the bay of Fundy. Those who are interested in this mill are making serious inquiries as to the amount of power that is available for the production of paper, and also as to the cost of this power.

Power Development
I could mention many other reasons why we are anxious to have power developed. I have spoken of them before in the house. Defence production is an example. We have not received in New Brunswick at any time our fair share of defence production. We believe that we would have received it if we had the necessary hydro development in the province.
I might ask the question, have we the prospective water power in New Brunswick? Anyone who has listened to hon. members from the maritime provinces debate this question during the last 10 or 15 years will realize that we have. I myself and other maritime members, particularly the opposition members, the former member for Cumberland, Mr. Black; the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Gillis) and other opposition members, have mentioned the Chignecto canal and the power that could be developed from the utilization of tidal waters. We have spoken of the Petitcodiac river and the Passa-maquoddy.
I mentioned the Passamaquoddy a few weeks ago. The United States, particularly the state of Maine, is greatly interested in the development of Passamaquoddy. They have asked the Dominion of Canada to join with them in an investigation into the feasibility of developing power at Passamaquoddy. As yet the Dominion of Canada has not indicated whether or not it is willing to assist in this investigation.
I am satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that Passamaquoddy will be developed by the United States if it is feasible, and I am satisfied that it will be of great benefit to the state of Maine, which lies side by side with the province of New Brunswick.
The development of power from the tides is not something altogether new. I remember reading a few years ago that in France they develop power from the tides. On the Severn river in England there is a power plant which gets its power from the rise and fall of the tide. That is also true of China. There is no place in the world that has such high tides and tremendous power potential and such tremendous rush of water as has the bay of Fundy in New Brunswick. These are just some of the possible developments that could take place in our province, some of which have been mentioned many times, I fear to very unsympathetic ears as far as the federal government is concerned.
I come now, Mr. Speaker, to a development which is under way at the present time, namely the Saint John river development. The development which is under way at the

present time, namely Beechwood, is only a part of the great possibilities for development of the Saint John river. This matter came up in the house a short time ago, and I was very disappointed to hear the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources- I should like to get his attention for a moment -say that it would not be the policy of the government to assist in the development of Beechwood. I should like to quote from his remarks at that time. This question was asked by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud), as reported at page 558 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. Has the government given consideration to the possibility of co-operating in the over-all power development of the Saint John river system in New Brunswick?
I may say the over-all power system means the development of Beechwood, the same as it does in other parts of the Saint John.

We need the development of Beechwood in the very worst way, but because they think it will bring some credit to Mr. Flemming, the premier of New Brunswick, they are trying to discredit it in every way they possibly can. I would ask those hon. members to be very careful and read over the report of the international committee on the development of the Saint John river and the development of Beechwood. I was discussing the attitude the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources took concerning the development of Beechwood.
He said, as reported at page 558 of Hansard of January 26:
All the way along there has been a constant exchange of views among provincial and federal technical and financial officials.

This is correct; there has been an exchange of views. He continued:
These discussions appeared to indicate that the development to the end of the Beeehwood phase could be carried out by the province of New Brunswick without jeopardizing its credit.
This is the point I wish to make, Mr. Speaker. It is not a matter of jeopardizing the credit of the province of New Brunswick; we did not expect the development of Beech-wood to jeopardize our credit. What the province of New Brunswick was asking for was assistance so we could get cheaper power. That is what jeopardizes the introduction of industry in our province. We did not in any way feel nor do we feel today that the development of power is jeopardizing our credit. The minister went on to say:
It appears, however, that future developments in the province are likely to require additional power on a substantial scale. This larger future development has been represented to the federal government as likely to be beyond the capacity of the province of New Brunswick to finance on its own.
Beeehwood is a part of the whole development of the Saint John river. There is no reason in the world why the federal government, if it is going to give assistance in the development of the Saint John river, could not give assistance to the whole scheme and not pick out parts of it and say we are doing this because it might jeopardize the finances of the province.
This attitude is jeopardizing our prospects of getting industry in that province. It is jeopardizing our prospects of being able to build a smelter in the northern part of our province, for instance. It is jeopardizing our prospects of developing our great pulp and paper industry there. I would ask the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources to reconsider this matter, and I am sure he will have the very grateful thanks of the people of my province if he does so.
There would be some difficulties and it would take some time to develop the whole of the Saint John river; there is no question about that. Some hon. members will recall that our good friend the former member for Temiscouata had his people so stirred up around lake Temiscouata that it would take considerable time, I am sure, to get the rights that we require in Quebec, for instance, in the development of other phases of the Saint John river. We have to get agreements with Maine. This will all take a long time, but we in New Brunswick cannot wait for all these things to be settled. We can produce power at Beeehwood now; we have the power plant almost constructed there, and that is where we need immediate assistance 67509-874

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I was discussing the development of Beech-wood on the Saint John river and the general development of the Saint John river for hydroelectric purposes. I was stating at that time that the Beeehwood development had been approved by the international joint commission, as well as outstanding engineers employed by the international joint commission from the United States and Canada, and also the engineering works group, which consisted of outstanding citizens from both the United States and Canada. This is a quotation from the report of the international joint commission:
The New Brunswick Electric Power Commission will be faced with a shortage of power in 1956 unless early steps are taken to deal with the situation.
As we all know, early steps were taken in the form of the development of Beeehwood by the present government of New Brunswick. It is also stated in this report:
If the economy of the province is to grow with the general growth of Canada as a whole, New Brunswick must be assured of future supplies of power at costs which are attractive to industry.
That really is the crux of the whole matter. The reason we have not been able to develop in New Brunswick is that we have lacked power. We shall develop in the future only if we have power at such a cost that it is attractive to industry. That is why appeals have gone out from the province of New Brunswick to the federal government for assistance in this matter. The engineering board of the international joint commission also stated that it-
-sees no objection to the construction of a plant at the Beeehwood site, as it would be a major part of any ultimate plan of development.
IMr. Brooks.]
These statements do away with the argument we have heard that Beeehwood should not have been developed until there was general development of the whole Saint John river area. At the opening of my remarks I dealt with the statement of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I am sorry he is not in the house.

subtopic: PARTICIPATION BY FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENTS
speechtext: Yes, he has been here since eight o'clock.

subtopic: PARTICIPATION BY FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
I beg your pardon. I should have said that he is not in his seat. The report of the Power Corporation of Canada Limited estimated:
. . . that power would be available at Beeehwood and before transmission for 5-4 mills per k.w.h. if interest costs were 5 per cent and that energy cost would be reduced to 31 mills per k.w.h. if capital was available at 21 per cent interest.
There is the very point that the people of New Brunswick, through the government of New Brunswick, are trying to make to the parliament of Canada. It is not that the finances of the province are going to be jeopardized, as the minister stated here some time ago, but the point is that we cannot encourage industry that is in the province and we cannot attract outside industry unless we can obtain our money at a cheaper rate of interest. We are not begging anything from the federal government. We are simply asking it to back our bonds so that with the credit of the dominion government behind us we may be able to borrow money at a cheaper rate of interest, which means all the difference between cheap and dear power in the province of New Brunswick. I want to impress that on the government, and particularly on the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
As I said before, the development at Beeehwood was approved by those people I mentioned. It was also approved by the Power Corporation of Canada Limited, by H. G. Acres Company Limited, and by the Shawinigan Engineering Company Limited. Those are three outstanding firms of consulting engineers in Canada. I want to say to my hon. friends from New Brunswick who belong to the Liberal party that not one of these firms I have mentioned, nor any creditable hydroelectric engineer in the Dominion of Canada or in the United States, has said that before Beeehwood is developed there must be development and storage in Maine and the province of Quebec. If any of those members speak later I would be pleased if they would give the names of any outstanding engineers who have ever made that statement.
At the outset of my remarks I spoke about the need. I know it is not necessary to develop that point here in this house. It has

been mentioned too often, and every hon. member is well aware of the situation in the maritime provinces as far as the requirements for hydroelectric development are concerned. Those provinces are starving for cheap hydroelectric power.
As for the advantages, I have also mentioned them. Power at a reasonable price would serve as a stimulus to all the province's industries at the present time. It would increase the industrialization of that province. It would help to develop our mineral deposits. It would help to develop further our pulp-wood industry. Another thing of very great importance to us in New Brunswick and the maritimes is that it would give employment to our young people and keep them at home. As I say, this is a very important matter as far as we are concerned. The tax revenues would be increased, as far as New Brunswick and the other maritime provinces are concerned.
There are other benefits. With the discovery of over 100 million tons of valuable ore in New Brunswick, it would give the province the greatest opportunity for economic expansion in its history. These mineral deposits can be developed in such a way as to be of maximum benefit to the people of New Brunswick only if there is a large surplus of relatively cheap electric power available. At the present time there is no surplus available, and the price of our power is too high. It is several times the Canadian average.
The chief reason for the high cost is the high rate of interest paid by the provincial government in borrowing money. A large surplus of relatively cheap power can be made available, which would develop the hydroelectric power potential of the province, with financial assistance by the federal government. There is no question at all about that.
Perhaps I might mention some precedents for consideration by the federal government as far as our problem is concerned. I think I could make a case in regard to the St. Lawrence seaway. We get very little, if any, benefit from the development of the St. Lawrence seaway. We in the maritime provinces will have to pay our full proportionate share of that development.

No nonsense about it. We hear so much about the trans-Canada pipe line. What benefit will the maritime provinces receive from that? Let no one say it is nonsense to say that we will receive no benefft. As a Canadian from the maritime provinces, may I say that we do not oppose these developments in other parts of Canada.
Power Development
We are glad to see the development of Canada, but we feel that we are entitled to some compensation when our money is paid out for the benefit of other parts of Canada and we receive absolutely no benefit.
Take the crown corporation that is being formed for the commercial development of atomic energy. It might very well have been established in the maritime provinces. We thought it was coming to the province of Nova Scotia. New Brunswick would not have objected to that, but instead it is being established here in the province of Ontario where there is a surplus of practically everything that goes to develop a country.
As I say, these are arguments that we could use, but *we do not intend to do so. We hope that out of pure justice to our own province and the other maritime provinces the government will give these matters due consideration.
Finally I wish to say that we are most sincere about this matter. I hope that all members from New Brunswick and the maritime provinces generally will add their voices to those who have already spoken. We are all interested because power is the key which will bring prosperity to that section of the dominion.
In the United States attention is being paid to what may be called depressed areas. We are not calling the maritimes a depressed area, but we might say that they are a neglected area. In the southern states of the United States and even in the New England states their atomic energy commission is locating many of their atomic reactors for commercial purposes. They are doing so in the New England states to bolster the economy of that part of their country. Why should these things not be done in Canada? We do not want a concentration of industry and people in the central provinces while on the extremities people are without industries and employment. It is not a healthy situation, and it is one which I believe can be corrected if the government will give serious consideration to the matter.
The proposal contained in the amendment is a very advanced step which would do a lot to improve the situation as far as that part of Canada is concerned. I do not think I need say any more, but I do hope the government will give every consideration to the amendment now before us. If they do I am sure they will be doing something which will be of great benefit to the part of the country from which I come.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment moved by the

Power Development
they are using for pulp purposes. The situation has reached the point where Nova Scotians are obliged to negotiate with a United States company in order to buy back some of their own pulpwood.
Of course, if a mill is to be established in this country, the location of that mill is not decided in Canada because the pulp and paper industry is largely in United States hands today to the extent, as I said before, that the uncut reserves are leased to them over a long period of time. That is true not only of pulp and paper but it is true also of automobiles, aluminium, nickel and the gold mines. We are losing our hold on our basic resources. It is true of iron ore and of steel to some considerable extent.
So when we are talking about developing our own resources we have to take a look at the leases we have granted to capital from the other side of the border. We do not have the say any more. In my opinion we have done a bad job of collective bargaining in farming out our natural resources. People talk about secession and going over to the United States. They do not have to go to the United States, because the United States has come over to them and in many ways they are calling the shots.
I know there were negotiations by the provincial government for some considerable time in connection with the pulp and paper development around Canso. It was hoped that a mill was going in there, but when the decision was made it was put somewhere else and that mill is going somewhere in Halifax county, although the best site was around the strait of Canso.
There is an organization functioning in the maritimes today that I consider one of the best developments since confederation, and that is the Atlantic economic council. Within the last few days I received one of their reports. They are studying this whole question. The governments of the maritime provinces have formed this economic council and staffed it with very able personnel. They are now studying the possibilities of developing the resources of Newfoundland, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, and how these provinces can best complement the economy of the other provinces. They have a committee on each of these resources, and on the question of power the committee make it quite clear in their report that they agree with what I am saying now so far as Nova Scotia is concerned. They are gathering a lot of data on this particular question of power. The committee say the power is there, and it is just a matter of getting some industries into the province to apply it.
[Mr. Gillls.l
There are things the government could do without this resolution, but they have not done them. For example, this government knows, and the provincial government knows, that the coal industry has lost about 3,000 people in the last couple of years. You would imagine that the government would be thinking there has to be something in that particular area to take up the slack. I appeal to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters).
For example, there is a fish plant at Morien which keeps a whole community of 3,000 or 4,000 people. It is the only industry in the area. If the breakwater which is there were expanded, and it would not cost a lot of money to put it in good shape, much greater room would be provided for boats. The basin comes right in from the sea and the storms are quite heavy. Larger boats and more boats could be used for fishing in that area, and the fish plant could be expanded greatly. I looked in the estimates but there is nothing for that purpose. You would not have to have any extra authority, because that is the prerogative of the Department of Public Works. The industry could be expanded because there is a market for those products.
Second, the town of Glace Bay is a town which has been hit by the closing of these mines. It has a population of 28,000 and there is a huge investment in churches, schools, and that sort of thing. There is a harbour there that is not in too bad shape. It is one of the best swordfishing grounds and during the season boats come in there from Lunenburg and all over Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. The harbour is small but it could be widened and deepened. It could be built up to accommodate twice the number of vessels that fish out of there now. This is the biggest swordfishing industry in North America and the catch goes to the United States, where it is a very expensive dish. This town has lost thousands of its population because of the closing of the mines.
The Minister of Public Works could very easily have said, well, there are two fish plants there that employ 600 to 700 people. The harbour does not accommodate very big boats, but if it were widened and dredged you could expand these fish plants so they would take up some of the slack from the waning coal industry. What is needed in most industrial communities is a source of auxiliary income.
In these homes around the steel plants and coal mines you will find two or three young women who cannot find employment in the community. Most such young women are employed in these fish plants and thus bring extra income into the home to supplement what the father is getting, perhaps from

unemployment insurance. There may be one man working in a home and supporting a family of eight or nine, many of them grown young women. The expansion of the breakwater at Morien and the widening and deepening of the Glace Bay harbour would do exactly the things I am saying. You do not have to have any extra authority to put something in the estimates of the Department of Public Works to cover those two items. I have talked about this for two years, but there still is not anything in the estimates.
As I said before, the Atlantic economic council is doing a good job. In time I believe we are going to be told through these organizations that we cannot continue to look to our Ontario and Quebec markets for the products of the maritime provinces. We will be told we have a market within the maritimes and we can trade within the maritimes. If that development takes places, then this part of the country is going to lose the lucrative market down there, but the maritime provinces are going to benefit 100 per cent. That is the purpose behind the formation of the Atlantic economic council and the industrial development boards. There are three of them, one in Glace Bay, one in Sydney and one in Antigonish county.
I realize that in time the basic industry of coal is going to peter out, especially when the gas line goes into Quebec and the Canadian National Railways completes the dieselization program. Something will have to take its place. I believe that pulp and paper at Canso is a natural. I believe that the expansion of steel production at the Sydney plant is the next step. I believe that in addition to turning out raw steel at that plant there should be a considerable amount of the steel fabricated in that area.
You know, just recently the capacity for raw steel at Stelco was pretty well taken up. They were shipping the raw material down to Sydney, and I suppose you were paying a freight subsidy on it. Dosco was turning out ingots and shipping them back up to Stelco again to be fabricated, and I suppose you were paying another subsidy on dragging them back to Hamilton.
I believe that Dosco is now considering the expansion of the steel plant at Sydney. It is a bit late; it should have been done a long time ago. Over the past 16 years many of us in the house have been urging that, because they have their own iron ore deposits at Wabana, Newfoundland. They do not have to depend on anything else. They have huge deposits there and all kinds of modern equipment for taking it from under the ground. It is only 90 miles from Newfoundland to the
Power Development
Sydney plant. They have their own coal mines next door to them. All the raw material necessary to turn out steel is right there. If there is any place in Canada where the manufacture of steel and steel fabrication should be going on at the cheapest possible rate it should be right in the Sydney area.
The United States steel people come all the way down to Quebec and drag their iron ore up from there to the head of the lakes. Dosco have their own ships, their own coal mines, their own gypsum deposits, their own limestone deposits; everything that goes into the manufacture of steel is right there at their back door, and they own it all. Why more raw steel is not made and more fabrication turned out there is a mystery to me. Perhaps there is a little too much United States capital in the steel industry today. I know four of the board of directors of Dosco are pretty big United States money men. They may have some influence in preventing the development of steel in that area, because perhaps it would interfere with their markets.
I trust the federal government will give some consideration to the setting up of this kind of a fund. It does not seem to me that there is any other way we are going to be able to work the resources-what is left of them- in this country. I cannot see any Canadian investors rushing in to develop areas like the iron ore deposits at Ungava and Labrador. They do not seem very anxious to get into textiles. That field is pretty well controlled in the United States. We do not seem to have people in this country who have enough confidence in the country to invest their money. The people of the United States are gamblers. They are doing it over there, and they are getting quite a control over our natural resources.
I think the discussion is timely. I am in hopes that when the Gordon commission reports we shall not treat it as we have treated other reports of commissions. The Sirois report was brought down in 1940. There were volumes and volumes of it. I do not think any hon. member could ever read it all. I picked out the parts that pertained to the maritime provinces. The Sirois report was a new constitution for Canada. It had everything that was necessary to the rehabilitation of the country, the development of its resources, an educational system, and so forth. But it went to the archives, as have the reports of commission after commission.
I hope when the Gordon commission reports -I trust the report will not be too lengthy, and that we shall all be able to read it-every hon. member will take it and have a square look at it and say to himself: "I represent

Power Development
Canada and Canadians. Every last recommendation in this report we are going to see implemented. I do not come from British Columbia or Ontario; I come from Canada". I hope that is the attitude we shall take; we are all Canadians and we want a balanced economy; we want the same educational advantages. If we have resources to be developed, Canada will pitch in and help develop them, and see that it is not made the responsibility of any particular province which may not be able to do it. We should all be glad to help one another. I hope that is the kind of approach we take to the Gordon report when we get it. I believe it is going to be a good one. The personnel of the commission are able men and will do and say the things that are right for this country when they report.
I was very pleased that the Leader of the Opposition brought on this discussion. Of course it is a socialist measure. I heard the leader of the C.C.F. party in 1942, 1943 and 1944 ask for the setting up of a development fund along the same lines and for the same purpose. But of course the Leader of the Opposition has been here a long while now. This is a bigger forum than the one he came from. He has heard all of those debates, and a lot of them have rubbed off on him. He himself is becoming a little socialistic, and I hope he will continue the attitude that he has taken this afternoon.
He put his discussion on a broad national base. You know, for some time I was afraid that he was supporting the kind of thing that is going on in this country, namely following the same pattern that has been carried on in the United States, developing the centre of the country and leaving the east and the west as the hewers of wood and the drawers of water. That is pretty well the development that we are getting in Canada. That is the kind of thing that Hitler was aiming at in Europe. He aimed to make Germany the super state with the supermen. He was going to use the rest of Europe as the hewers of wood and the drawers of water, the suppliers of raw material and brawn. The Germans were going to preside over them as the great super race, and they were going to keep the rest of the continent in slavery.
Well, if you look at the United States you will find that the centre is rich. They have everything they require. But if you go to the south you will find they still have the thatched roof and the tarpaper shacks. If you go into the New England states, if you drive through there, you will find that they are no better off than they are in the maritime provinces, and maybe not as well off,

because there has not been very much industrial development taking place in that part of the country. Let us not follow the backward pattern that was set in other countries a long time ago when perhaps it was all right, when you had to concentrate population.
Today we are in a different position. Today it should be the aim in Canada to put every section of this country on exactly the same basis for every purpose. It is a bad development both socially and economically to build up the centre as we have in Ontario and not so much in Quebec, where problems are being created. There are sections of Ontario today that are screaming for relief from school and housing problems. People are being dumped in there both through immigration and migration from other provinces. That has happened to such an extent that they are not able to handle them and provide the necessary services, hospitalization, schools and so forth. The premier of Ontario said that himself on several occasions.
I do not think any country will ever be great until everybody in it shares equally in the wealth of the country. I hope we have made a start by this amendment of the Leader of the Opposition. I rise to speak in this debate because it focuses attention on one of the factors involved in our economic development. Several members who have already spoken have stressed the relationship between power development and economic development generally, and it is to that particular phase of the question that I should like to address some of my remarks.
A great industrialist, Cyrus Eaton, made the remark that industry springs where power is, especially where cheap electric power is. It is true that the availability of power at competitive rates is a factor of first rate importance in the location of particular industries; and it is true, of course, that power is of secondary importance in the location of other industries.
It is important, in discussing power in its relation to economic development, to realize

that it is simply one of several decisive factors in industrial location. Any consulting firm would certainly regard location near valuable raw materials, location near important markets and, certainly, location near suitable labour skills as equally important with power in the development of any industry, or in some cases much more important. So in presenting any argument on the importance of power one must conclude that it is a necessary condition, but not a sufficient condition, of industrial location.
In Nova Scotia, and to some extent in several of the other eastern provinces, we have exhausted our hydroelectric possibilities. We have as a result been accustomed to attribute our slower rate of economic development to the lack of hydroelectric possibilities in the maritime provinces. There has been in existence in Nova Scotia and elsewhere in the maritime provinces a very real feeling that the scarcity of power, and especially the lack of power at what are regarded as competitive rates, is one of the chief causes of the slower rate of economic development.
I do not intend to review the problem fully, but I think I should say enough to indicate that all the studies I have seen on the economic development of the maritime provinces indicate that the lack of power at competitive rates is not of crucial importance in the economic development of the eastern provinces. One of the studies I have at hand was conducted by Professor Keirstead of McGill University shortly after the war, when he was asked to investigate the probable economic effects of the war on the maritime provinces of Canada. One of the subjects to which he addressed himself was this particular subject of power and industrial development. He made this comment:
Power costs have often been regarded, particularly in industries like pulp and paper, as of decisive importance in determining location advantage. Our evidence suggests the possibility of exaggerating the importance of power as a location factor.
Later on in his analysis of the pulp and paper industry Professor Keirstead gives some rather convincing evidence. He states that the power costs, for example, of a median establishment in Quebec are some 5 per cent lower than a similar establishment in Nova Scotia, and further that in pulp and paper, to carry out his illustration, power costs are one-fifteenth of the total cost of production, so that the general advantage that a Quebec competitor would enjoy over a Nova Scotian competitor would be something like -33 per cent per ton output. Therefore the conclusion is inescapable that in this particular instance, which may be
Power Development
applicable to other industries, power is not and has not been a decisive determinant in industrial location.
To bring the discussion up to present day evidence, I was interested, like the hon. member for Cape Breton South, in reading some of the arguments presented by the Atlantic provinces economic council in a report issued just recently. I share the views the hon. member for Cape Breton South has expressed with respect to this new organization in the Atlantic provinces. One of the first duties undertaken by it was to set up a power committee to examine the power situation in the Atlantic provinces. Because it is of some interest I might mention that the chairman of the power committee is Mr. R. E. Tweeddale, assistant chief engineer of the New Brunswick Power Commission. The committee made what must be regarded as a preliminary study of the power situation in the Atlantic provinces, and this is the result of their preliminary study. They say:
Basically, there is an adequate supply of electric power available In the maritime region to meet present demands. The committee believes that electric power can be made available for any section of the region to meet future demands.
Then the committee looked into the competitive relationship of power costs in the maritime provinces and other areas. It is true that power costs are higher in the Atlantic provinces than in the central provinces, but the committee states that power rates in the Atlantic provinces are not out of line with power rates on the eastern seaboard of the United States, and there it is not argued that power has been a decisive determinant of industrial location. To argue thus is to say that power has not been a decisive determinant of industrial location, but I think it is true that if you combine our lack of competitive advantage in power with some of our other disadvantages, namely our distance from national markets and the high costs of transportation, you may have more illuminating reasons for the relative lack of economic growth in the Atlantic provinces. It may be that if we could develop very cheap power for distribution in the Atlantic provinces it would be a compensating factor that would make up for our evident disadvantages in geography.
In Nova Scotia, of course, we must depend on coal for power generation. Our hydroelectric possibilities are exhausted, and it would be unrealistic to consider the generation of power from any other source. I must say that the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys has been alive to the importance of the coal industry in the generation of power in the maritime provinces. The hon. member for Cape Breton South has referred

to the investigation made by Professor Christie into thermal power generation in the Atlantic provinces. In his report Professor Christie did make a very important suggestion which is worthy of study by the provincial governments of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
He suggested a single power authority to administer the private and public power companies in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. This single power authority would be completely responsible for the generation and distribution of power in these two provinces. He further suggested that this interconnecting system might be linked with the system in northern Maine and that in the part of Quebec on the New Brunswick border.
He claimed very outstanding advantages for this proposal. It would join the hydro and coal electrical generating systems and would permit the development of larger plants with very evident economies in operation. It would follow that there would be a cheaper electrical rate with a very reliable source of distribution. This is one of the interesting proposals that came out of Professor Christie's study, and one that is certainly in line with the need of developing the electrical possibilities in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick and in line with the requirements of the coal industry.
This afternoon the Leader of the Opposition referred to the problem of underground gasification of coal. This is a problem which has been the subject of considerable study by various organizations. I have, for example, the annual report for 1951 of the Nova Scotia research foundation, which contains a rather technical discussion of the experimental difficulties in developing this process for commercial utilization. While experiments have apparently been conducted in various countries, no country has yet succeeded in bringing this development to commercial utilization, and I think the reason is that they have been unable to solve the combustion process so that they get a gas of sufficient heat.
But while the underground gasification of coal cannot at present be a practical possibility, there is another form of gasification of coal that I think has advanced to a more satisfactory stage. I refer to the surface gasification of coal. There have been experiments undertaken at Morgantown, West Virginia, by the department of mines of Washington, and they now have in existence and in commercial use surface plants which do gasify coal. I understand there are several of these plants in operation in that part of the United States.
fMr. MacEachen.]

Its implications for the power industry and also for the coal industry of Nova Scotia are very evident. If we had a unit that could gasify, for example, 7,000 tons of coal a day, and I think that is one of the economical units, we would have a market that would absorb maybe 3 million tons of Nova Scotia coal a year. If we did that, what effect would it have on the annual expenditures we make today in subventions for the movement of coal from Cape Breton? Here is something that we should look into.
You may then ask this question. If you gasify this coal, what do we do to dispose of the gas? This, of course, would require a type of development that would bring this gas to the more populous centres of Canada. If it were economical to send gas up to Quebec, for example, it would be certainly a practical possibility because of the stability it would provide to the Nova Scotia coal industry and because of the more useful way in which to expend this annual amount of money that is now spent on subventions.
This is one of the more promising experiments now going on in the United States. In the next few months or the next few years I am sure we are going to hear a good deal more about this experiment that is now going on at Morgantown, and that may have important implications for the coal industry of the province of Nova Scotia.
This amendment is an interesting one. It focuses attention on one of the elements of industrial development. It leaves unmentioned several of the others. At the present stage the proposal does not appear to be a certain way of assisting in the particular economic disabilities of the Atlantic provinces.

Mr. Speaker, when the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) was speaking on the question of development in Edmonton last September he had this to say, and I quote his words:
Canada stands at the threshold of expansion unequalled in our history. We believe that if we can maintain a vigorous and expanding economy.

and if we can create the conditions under which Canadians can avail themselves of the great opportunities this country presents, then none of us need fear for his future or for the future of the nation.
Who is going to quarrel with that statement of the Prime Minister? Certainly not the Conservative party, because we have been trying to convince the government of the common sense and factuality of these economic facts of life, and to persuade them to act on those facts. All we wish is that the Prime Minister and his colleagues would act as confidently as they speak, and that their actions were as bold as their words.
As the Prime Minister has said, this country presents tremendous opportunities. But opportunities do not just come to you. Opportunities must be seized. As he said, we in Canada are on the threshold of an unequalled expansion. But, Mr. Speaker, thresholds must be crossed. They do not just stand there waiting for you. The possibilities which the Prime Minister outlined will become realities only if we have imaginative planning and action by business, industry and, not least of all, the Prime Minister's own government. What, I ask you, is this government doing to promote this country's expansion? What strong and visible foundation is this government placing under Canada's future?

This project seems to illustrate a truth that is too often forgotten-that any contribution to the Canadian economy is a contribution to all of Canada and not just to the area immediately concerned.
Mr. Speaker, that is, of course, perfectly true. But why is this government at present engaged only on the St. Lawrence seaway? Why is it not pushing ahead with similar projects of similar magnitude, which would have similar benefits in other parts of the country?

land which today is wheat-growing land but which then will become market-gardening land. This will greatly diversify and improve the agricultural economy of Saskatchewan. The credit, sir, of this country is good. It will not be strained one iota by borrowing the capital necessary for the basic development of this country. kind I have mentioned. The people of this country have just as much faith in the future of this country as the Prime Minister professes to have. If he will act with vigour and imagination, he will find that the people of this country will back him up.

Industries establish themselves in certain localities for two maih reasons. The first is because they believe that their cost of production will be lower than otherwise, and the second is because they believe their cost of distribution will be lower, and that they will be able to make more rapid deliveries of their finished products to their customers.
Power is a very important component of any cost, and the reason a very high proportion of industry in this country has so far concentrated in Ontario and Quebec is simply because there has been an abundance of cheap electric power in both those provinces. If equally cheap power could be developed in important quantities in the maritimes and in the west, then branch plants would be located in those areas because it would be to the advantage of industry to locate there.
The advantages industry will derive are three in number. First, they will have a power cost as cheap as anywhere else in the country. Second, they will make tremendous savings because their cost of distribution will be lower than if they have to pay for the long freight haul from central Canada to the west or the maritimes. Third, the time of delivery of the finished article will be out down considerably, and under today's competitive economic conditions, that is a very important factor.
If the decentralization of industry could be made a reality as a result of the adoption of the policies outlined by the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon; if we could develop cheaper sources of electric power in all parts of this country, then our whole economy would be strengthened. It would be strengthened because the west and the maritimes would be less dependent on their

primary products, and their individual economies would become more stable.
Another thing I believe we must do to strengthen our economy, and increase employment and prosperity right across this country is, as the Leader of the Opposition has urged on many occasions, that this government should give the lead in promoting the processing of far more of our primary products right here in Canada. It is almost unbelievable, but it is a fact, that we seem quite content to ship most of our primary products out of the country in their raw state, to feed the mass producing machines of the United States and other countries. Then we turn around and buy back many of those raw materials in their finished form.
There is no reason at all why a far larger proportion of our raw materials should not be turned into the finished article by Canadian workmen working in Canadian plants. If people from the United States, from Britain, from Germany and others can take Canadian raw materials, turn them into finished products, and find a ready market throughout the world for those products, then there is no reason in the world why Canadians, working with Canadian raw materials in Canadian plants cannot find just as good a market in other parts of the world as do people of other nationalities who use our raw materials today.
What we need is some action, once again, by this lethargic government. We want the government to give a lead to industry in two ways; first of all by sponsoring a greatly expanded industrial research program, and second by revising its taxation policies so that new industries will be induced to start up, and present industries will be induced to expand.
Mr. Speaker, we know-everyone of us knows-that we have right here in Canada everything that is needed for a tremendous industrial expansion. We have enough food to feed several times our present population. We have almost unbelievable supplies of timber and iron ore, which are the basic requirements of any industrial program. We have almost unbelievable resources of every kind of power; we have tremendous resources of practically every metal that is needed in industry, nickel, lead, zinc, copper. With regard to power, in the province of Saskatchewan we have not a single hydroelectric plant. All our power is produced either from coal, from gas or from diesel power. We want cheaper power in Saskatchewan because we want to see more diversification in that province. Diversification has been going on fairly rapidly during the last few years, and it is predicted in Saskatchewan that in the next ten years, provided we can produce enough power, the so-called wheat economy of Saskatchewan will be completely changed.
We need not only power in our province; we need irrigation. Tonight the hon. member for Medicine Hat told us something about an irrigation project in his province. Last summer I had the good fortune to go through a large part of the irrigated sections of that province. I went into the Vauxhall district about which the hon. member spoke. I wish to take the house back some 50 years, or a little over 50 years, because I was in that district in the year 1905. At that time settlers

Power Development
were few and far between. What settlers there were were scattered along the different rivers.
In those days the cattle population was small because of the fact that there was no water available except in the rivers. They could travel a distance of only about 10 miles for feed because that was about all the distance they could go. Most of the time the cattle were walking back and forth to the river to drink. They never did get very fat. At that time it was considered that it took at least a quarter section of land to feed one cow.
That was the siutation in 1905. I might say that hay was almost not to be found at all, The rancher I worked with at that time thought he was lucky if he could cut a load of hay by keeping his mowing machine going all day. He had to haul it 15 or 20 miles. There were no trees. There was one small bush which was called the lone tree that you could see for 20 miles in all directions. There was no growth; there were no farms; there was nothing but a huge expanse of country that was not worth anything to anybody.
I left that country with a wagon train in 1905. We moved up into what they called the long grass country. Last summer eleven of us decided that since it was 50 years since we left that Vauxhall country, we would like to go back and take a look at it. We did. We went on to Provost and straight south from Provost. After we got about 50 miles from Provost we ran out of farming communities. From there on, almost into Medicine Hat, down to Suffield we saw a few deserted homes.
We stopped and looked at one of the homes that had been deserted. It looked like it had been a pretty nice house. In that house was a piano. When the people who had been there left, no doubt they did not have room on their wagons to carry away the piano, and so the piano was left. The following day we got into the Brooks country.
I am telling the story because, as I said when I opened my remarks, I want to get more members on the government side of the house interested in irrigation. The transformation that has taken place in that area is almost unbelievable. For somebody who left there 50 years ago and went back, the change was almost unbelievable. There was no town of Brooks at that time. There was a section house there and a few section men working on the tracks. There was a small post office, and the postmaster had $200 or $300 worth of groceries. It was very seldom that he had a customer outside of the section-men.
Today there is a town of several thousand inhabitants. Surrounding that town for many miles is one of the finest agricultural districts to be found anywhere in Canada. Instead of cattle walking 10 miles to get their feed and 10 miles back to get their water, cattle and sheep by the thousands are standing knee deep in alfalfa. They have to move only a few feet to get a drink of water. All they have to do is grow and get fat, and believe me that is what they are doing. We have a half million acres in the province of Saskatchewan that could be developed in just the same way, provided we could get the assistance of the federal government.
I said a few moments ago that it was considered it took at least a quarter section to feed a cow. Cattlemen in particular are vitally interested in irrigation. I came across an article in the Country Guide which told a story illustrating this point. It is a long story concerning irrigation in Alberta. I have not time to go into it, but I do want to read one little part to show what can be done with irrigation in the production of cattle:
The eyes of cattlemen have been recenly focused on irrigated pasture. Because of this, two areas of 500 acres each, five miles east of Hays, have been fenced, broken and seeded to grass mixtures for use as community pastures. Jim Wickenheiser, for one, is planning to buy a flock of sheep. Others are planning on cattle and sheep too, for pasture marketed through livestock can always be sold, and promises good returns per acre.
There is plenty of evidence that this might offer the best hope for these new areas. For instance, W. W. Foss, P.F.R.A. chief engineer at Lethbridge, returned from a tour of U.S. projects in 1954 and said, "I was amazed to find, even in the fabulously rich irrigated valleys of California, grain and livestock as the major sources of income. In all projects an average of about two-thirds of the acreage is devoted to them."
Bight in Canada, at Kamloops, B.C., the range experimental station has produced up to 800 pounds of beef per acre from irrigated pasture. At the Lethbridge experimental station, up to 6,100 pounds of fluid milk have been produced in a year from an acre, while at Broxburn, Alberta, 80 Aberdeen-Angus cows and their calves thrived on only 20 acres last summer.
That illustrates what can be done in the raising of livestock when we have irrigation. Irrigation is not good for cattle production only; there are many different kinds of crops that can be grown on irrigated land.
I have in my hand a press clipping which contains a little story about two young men who came to Canada from the United States:
Dick Butler and Robert Faris were bom and raised in the potato and corn areas of Idaho. They'd done well for themselves but early this spring decided they wanted to do better. They thought sheep raising in Canada or South America would be a good bet.
IMr. Campbell.]

They came to Canada and Mr. Faris is reported to have said:
"When we saw the Bow Island district this spring while looking for sheep land and we heard that irrigation was in sight for this year, we decided that there was no place on earth with better possibilities."
They went right to work and before long had possibly the largest single acreage of dry beans in the British empire, 600 acres of them.
The entire crop is certified seed and they have already made arrangements with neighbours to supply them with seed for the coming year.
"The average Canadian eats 12 pounds of beans per year, while an American eats 15 pounds with the Mexican being at the top with 55 pounds per person per year," said Mr. Faris.
"According to Alberta government statistics, this province imports practically all beans consumed and is presently short about 35,000 acres," he says.
Looking over his first year's crop which he thought wasn't very good Mr. Faris after conversing with his partner said it would go nearly 1,800 pounds to the acre.
"Even if we get a very low price of seven to eight cents a pound," he claimed, "we stand to clear about $100 an acre and where can you beat that."
That is all I want to say this evening, Mr. Speaker, but I do want to urge the government and hon. members on the other side of the house to take another look at the South Saskatchewan river dam and irrigation project. I know that the Prime Minister has been blamed in the newspapers for being the one who opposed this project, but I understand he has been through that part of the country and has seen something of what can be done there. I am hoping he will use his influence to try and see if something can be done in the near future to give Saskatchewan this project.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PARTICIPATION BY FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
Before we proceed to the adjournment of the house I should like to say a few words just for the purpose of informing hon. members of the way I look at the situation.
Power Development
I should like to refer again to the amendment that has been moved. It refers to a joint investment program for the development of power resources in any province where the government of such province requests the co-operation of the government in carrying out such developments.
Some hon. members have already indicated that this amendment is very wide and at least one hon. member, the hon. member for Cape Breton South, referred to a resolution of his on the order paper, a notice of motion which is notice No. 3, which asks for direct government assistance for the establishment of additional or alternative industries in the areas concerned. No doubt he had also in mind, like I have, the notice of motion in the name of the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, No. 24, and the one in the name of the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska, No. 27, both of which deal with the consideration to be given by the government to the advisability of providing assistance to the province of New Brunswick in the development of electric power.
It seems to me that some of these notices of motion when they are called, and if they are called between now and the end of the present session, might have been included in the discussion which is now before this house. I do not want to apply the rule of anticipation, but I think hon. members who may feel that the present amendment could block their own notice of motion at a later stage might do well to take advantage of the present debate so that later when their own notice of motion comes along they may be satisfied that having dealt with the substance in this debate, they will not again press their own notice of motion. '
The amendment is so wide that I do not feel I should use citation 350 of Beauchesne's third edition, which is to the effect that it is out of order to move, as an amendment to another question, a motion standing on the order paper as a notice of motion. Therefore, having said that, I hope hon. members will govern themselves accordingly because we do not want to have overlapping of debate or repetition.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.

subtopic: COLLECTIVE AGREEMENT CONTRACTS

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: COLLECTIVE AGREEMENT CONTRACTS
speechtext:
1.	How many collective agreements between employers and employees in Canada now include a provision lor a guaranteed wage?
2.	How many employees are covered by such contracts?
3.	How many ol such contracts were negotiated during 1954? How many since January 1, 1955?
4.	What relationship exists between such provisions for a guaranteed annual wage and unemployment insurance? Has it been made clear in the unemployment insurance regulations that any payments received from an employer under a guaranteed annual wage plan by an employee not working at the time are not regarded as earnings within the meaning of the Unemployment Insurance Act?
5.	Is the Department of Labour taking any steps to encourage more employers and employees to include provision for a guaranteed annual wage in their collective agreements? If so, what are such steps?
6.	Are there available any departmental studies on the subject of the guaranteed annual wage?
Answer by: Mr. Gregg:
1.	Since the signing last June in the United States of the first guaranteed wage plan in which payments are to be integrated with unemployment insurance payments, five agreements containing plans of a similar nature, frequently known as supplementary unemployment benefit plans, have been negotiated covering Canadian firms.
The department has, in addition, record of five agreements under which a minimum amount of work or wages is guaranteed during the year without reference to unemployment insurance. Three of these are plans of several years' standing. The other two are more recent plans which guarantee a minimum number of weeks of work during the year.
Thus, total plans including both types, of which the department has knowledge, number ten.
2.	The five agreements containing plans of the supplementary unemployment benefit type integrated with unemployment insurance cover 8,261 employees.
The other five agreements containing a guaranteed annual wage plan by our definition cover 1,578 employees.
In total then, 9,839 employees are covered by the ten agreements.
3.	None of the contracts of which the Department of Labour has knowledge were negotiated during 1954. All of the five plans
providing for supplementary payments to unemployment insurance have been negotiated since January 1, 1955.
Of the other five plans, three were negotiated several years ago and two have been negotiated since January 1, 1955.
4.	Since the provisions of guaranteed annual wage plans differ considerably, each plan must be studied before its relationship to the Unemployment Insurance Act can be determined. No specific regulation refers to guaranteed annual wage plans as such. Therefore the unemployment insurance commission would not be in a position to determine whether or not payments received under any particular plan will or will not be regarded as earnings within the meaning of the act until the provisions of that plan are fully considered in the light of all the provisions of the act and regulations.
5.	The Department of Labour does not attempt to encourage or influence management or labour to seek any particular working condition in collective agreements. It is the policy of the department that working conditions should be negotiated freely and directly by the parties concerned.
6.	The only published study on this subject appeared in the September 1953 issue of the Labour Gazette. In that study five agreements were shown as containing annual work or wage guarantees. Three of these are still in existence and are included in the ten agreements having a guarantee as noted above. The plans in the other two agreements in the 1953 study were subsequently deleted from the agreements. Other studies on this subject will be made in due course as warranted.

subtopic: ARCHBISHOP BORIS OP RUSSIA

speechtext: Question No. 138

subtopic: ARCHBISHOP BORIS OP RUSSIA
speechtext:
1.	Was Archbishop Boris and his party, during their recent trip in Canada, at any time guests of the federal government or any official thereof?
2.	If so, did the government acquaint itself with the background and activities of Archbishop Boris and/or his party?
3.	Was there anything which could cause any hesitation in granting visas and what was the position and official status in the U.S.S.R. of the members of the party?
4.	Did the government inquire as to whether or not visas had been refused by the United States and France to Archbishop Boris or any member of his party?
5.	If so, with what result?
6.	How long was this party travelling in Canada, at what port did they enter, what was their point of departure, and did any government official or officials accompany the party on their tour?
7.	Did the party or any member thereof travel under diplomatic immunity?
8.	Was the entry of the archbishop and his party recommended to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration or any other department of the government? If so, by whom, and did the recommendation state the purpose of the visit?

Answer by: Mr. Pearson:
1.	No.
2.	Answered by No. 1.
3.	No. All requests for visas are carefully scrutinized. The government was supplied with the usual particulars about the individual members of this group, and after the normal consideration by the appropriate Canadian authorities it was decided that visas could be authorized. The official positions of the members of the party were:
Vik, Boris Ivanovich-
Archbishop, Russian Orthodox church.
Ruzitsky, K. I.-
Archpriest, rector of Moscow ecclesiastical
academy.
Gorbatchev, A. P.-
Inspector of Moscow ecclesiastical academy
(a layman).
4 and 5. The United States permitted the archbishop to visit the United States early in 1955, and again issued him a visa in November, 1955, on the understanding that he would minister only to soviet nationals in the United States. Proceedings were taken to cancel this visa, however, when the Soviet union insisted that he be allowed to enter on a permanent basis to exercise the administrative functions of exarch of the Russian Orthodox church in the United States. Since the archbishop wished to come to Canada for a short
Questions
visit only, the United States reasons for refusing him entry did not apply to Canada. Our embassy in Washington was in touch with the state department on this subject. The government did not inquire as to whether visas had been refused by France to Archbishop Boris or any member of his party.
6.	The party travelled in Canada for two weeks, entering on December 4 at Montreal and leaving on December 18, also from Montreal. No government official accompanied the party on its tour.
7.	No. Members of the party were given ordinary non-immigrant visas.
8.	Yes. The general council of the United Church of Canada recommended the entry of the archbishop and his party. The secretary of the general council stated in a letter to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that the object of the visit would be "to establish friendly relations between various communions of the Christian church, to increase our knowledge of one another's problems and to consider some aspects of the general subject of the church and international affairs with which we are all deeply concerned." The request for visas was passed to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration with an explanation of the purpose of the visit, and that department approved the request subject to the normal requirements for non-immigrant entry.
